title: Judges 6:1–10
context: Judges 6:1–10 begins the Gideon cycle with the familiar pattern: Israel does evil, and the LORD gives them into Midian’s hand for seven years. Midianites, Amalekites and eastern peoples sweep in at harvest like locusts, so Israel hides in caves and is brought very low. When Israel cries out, the LORD first sends an unnamed prophet who recounts the exodus and the gift of the land and charges that Israel has not listened to his voice. Both traditions see God’s discipline, his attention to his people’s cry, and his call to repentance before deliverance.

verses.text: The children of Israel did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, so the LORD delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel does evil in the LORD’s sight, and the LORD gives them into Midian’s hand for seven years. Arminians read the familiar cycle of Judges as God responding justly to his people’s repeated choice to turn from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the LORD himself hands Israel over, so the oppression is his discipline, not a sign that he has lost control. Both traditions read the verse as covenant discipline aimed at bringing Israel back, as in Judges 2:11–19.

verses.text: The hand of Midian prevailed against Israel; and because of Midian the children of Israel made themselves the dens which are in the mountains, the caves, and the strongholds.
verses.arminianNotes: Midian prevails, and Israel hides in mountain dens, caves and strongholds. Arminian readers see how far the people have fallen: those who were given cities and fields now live in hiding because of their disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the contrast with the conquest under Joshua. Both traditions read the verse as showing the misery that comes from covenant unfaithfulness, and they see it preparing for the deliverance God will provide.

verses.text: So it was, when Israel had sown, that the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east came up against them.
verses.arminianNotes: Whenever Israel had sown, Midianites, Amalekites and eastern peoples came up against them. Arminians note the cruelty of the raids, timed to take the harvest after Israel’s labor, which made the oppression economic as well as military.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The "children of the east" are desert peoples from beyond the Jordan. Both traditions read the verse as describing a seasonal raiding pattern that left Israel’s work fruitless, a reversal of the promised blessing on obedience (compare Deuteronomy 28:33).

verses.text: They encamped against them, and destroyed the increase of the earth, until you come to Gaza. They left no sustenance in Israel, and no sheep, ox, or donkey.
verses.arminianNotes: They camped against Israel, destroyed the land’s produce as far as Gaza, and left no food or livestock. Arminian readers see the completeness of the devastation, reaching across the land to the coast, as a measure of how serious Israel’s situation had become.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the covenant warnings in Deuteronomy 28 include enemies eating the land’s produce. Both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of those warnings and as preparing for God’s mercy.

verses.text: For they came up with their livestock and their tents. They came in as locusts for multitude. Both they and their camels were without number; and they came into the land to destroy it.
verses.arminianNotes: They came with livestock, tents and countless camels, like locusts, to destroy the land. Arminians read the locust image as describing both the multitude and the destructiveness of the raiders, who stripped the land as a swarm would.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The mention of camels shows a mobile raiding force that Israel could not easily resist. Both traditions read the image as stressing that Israel is helpless on its own, so that deliverance will clearly be the LORD’s work.

verses.text: Israel was brought very low because of Midian; and the children of Israel cried to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel was brought very low and cried to the LORD. Arminian readers see the people turning to God in distress and God listening to them, which shows his readiness to respond to his people’s cry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the cry is not described as repentance, and the following verses show God addressing their sin. Both traditions see God’s mercy toward his people even when their cry comes mainly from suffering.

verses.text: When the children of Israel cried to the LORD because of Midian,
verses.arminianNotes: When Israel cried to the LORD because of Midian, his first answer is not a deliverer. Arminians see God treating the cry seriously and addressing its root, Israel’s sin, before he sends deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The verse is a short transition that connects the cry with the prophet’s message. Both traditions read it as showing that God answers his people in the way they need, which here means confronting them with his word.

verses.text: The LORD sent a prophet to the children of Israel; and he said to them, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘I brought you up from Egypt, and brought you out of the house of bondage.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sends an unnamed prophet who reminds Israel that he brought them up from Egypt and out of the house of bondage. Arminians see God appealing to his past grace as a reason for Israel to return to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the message begins with what God has done, not with what Israel must do. Both traditions read the exodus as the foundation of Israel’s covenant obligation and see the prophet calling the people back on that basis.

verses.text: I delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out from before you, and gave you their land.
verses.arminianNotes: God delivered Israel from the Egyptians and all their oppressors, drove out the nations, and gave them the land. Arminian readers see the list of God’s acts as showing how undeserved Israel’s ingratitude was, since every good thing they had came from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a summary of God’s faithfulness to his promises. Both traditions read the prophet’s review of history as emphasizing God’s grace before he names Israel’s sin in the next verse.

verses.text: I said to you, “I am the LORD your God. You shall not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.” But you have not listened to my voice.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: God had told Israel not to fear the gods of the Amorites, but they have not listened to his voice. Arminians read the charge as Israel’s responsibility for choosing idols, and see the prophet calling them to repent before deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree on the charge. The prophet’s message ends without a promise, and the deliverance that follows is God’s free mercy. Both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s grace and his call to obedience go together.
